passages.text: When Peter had said these things, the woman stopped in her tracks and, as though from shock, fainted. Peter came over and paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind, trying to persuade her to say what exactly it was that she was suffering. Though as if drunk, with the rest of her body gone limp, she recovered herself enough to be able to bear the magnitude of the joy she was anticipating. Rubbing her own face, she said, “Where is this young man?” Peter, who by now had discerned the whole situation, said, “You tell me first—for otherwise you cannot see him.” In her eagerness she said, “I am the young man’s mother.” Peter said, “What is his name?” She replied, “Clement.” Peter said, “It is he. He was the one who spoke with me a short while ago, whom I instructed to wait for me in the ship.” Falling at Peter’s feet, she begged him to hurry to the ship. Peter said, “If you keep our agreement, I will do this too.” She said, “I will do everything; only show me my only child, for through him I will feel that I am seeing my two children who died here.” Peter said, “When you see him, remain quiet until we have left the island.” She said, “I will do so.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: stopped in her tracks and, as though from shock, fainted
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιστήσασα marks her coming to a halt, while ἀπέψυξεν here describes a collapse or loss of consciousness rather than literal death.

lexical_decisions.chosen: paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The absolute ἐπισχών can mean that Peter paused or waited; the context could alternatively suggest that he supported or steadied her. νήφειν denotes recovering mental clarity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the rest of her body gone limp
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase depicts bodily relaxation or loss of strength, in keeping with the comparison to drunkenness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she recovered herself enough to be able to bear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual sequence of infinitives expresses her recovery for the purpose or result of enduring the anticipated joy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If you keep our agreement
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνθήκας denotes agreed terms or conditions, referring to Peter’s requirement that she remain composed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my only child
lexical_decisions.rationale: μονογενές presents Clement as her unique or sole remaining child in this context; the more formally literal “only-born child” would sit awkwardly beside the immediately mentioned two deceased children.

passages.text: Peter therefore took her by the hand and led her toward the ship. When I saw him leading a woman by the hand, I laughed; and I came over and, out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place. The moment I touched her hand, she gave a great cry like a mother, wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me, her son, with kisses. Knowing nothing of the whole situation, I shook her off as though she were mad; yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τιμὴν αὐτοῦ ἀντ’ αὐτοῦ χειραγωγεῖν αὐτὴν ἐπειρώμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place
lexical_decisions.rationale: Clement attempts to relieve Peter of the task as an expression of honor or respect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she gave a great cry like a mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀλολύζω denotes a loud, emotionally charged cry; the comparison explicitly characterizes it as maternal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me with kisses
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπλέκομαι describes an enclosing embrace, while the intensive καταφιλέω conveys repeated or ardent kissing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: me, her son
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative phrase stands in apposition to με and identifies Clement from the mother’s perspective.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰδούμενος δὲ καὶ τὸν Πέτρον ἐπικραινόμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἰδέομαι with Peter as its object expresses regard or deference; the imperfect of πικραίνω describes Clement’s growing vexation.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let her be! What are you doing, child Clement, shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you?” When I heard this, I became covered in tears; and I fell upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down, and showered her with kisses. For as soon as this was said to me, I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance. Many crowds therefore came running to learn about the woman who had been begging, saying to one another, “Her son, a man of distinction, has recognized her.” When we wished to leave the island at once with my mother, she said, “My longed-for child, it is right to say farewell to the woman who took me in. She is poor and completely disabled and lies at home.” When Peter heard this, he marveled, as did all the surrounding crowds, at the woman’s noble disposition. Peter immediately ordered some men to go and carry the woman in on a cot. And likewise, when she had been brought in and the cot had been set down, Peter said in the hearing of all the crowds, “If I am indeed a herald of truth, then, as grounds for faith among those standing by, so that they may know that there is one God, the one who made the world, let her rise immediately in health.” As soon as Peter said this, the woman rose, having been healed. She fell before Peter, and after showering her familiar friend with kisses, she asked what this might mean. Her friend briefly related to her the whole event of the recognition, and those who heard it were astounded. Then the mother, seeing that her hostess had been healed, asked that she too might receive healing. Peter laid his hand on her and healed her as well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄντως emphasizes that she is genuinely Clement’s birth mother, while ἀποσείω recalls his attempt to push her away.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I became covered in tears
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίδακρυς depicts Clement as tearful all over or streaming with tears.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμαυρῶς marks the memory as indistinct, and the imperfect suggests an emerging recollection.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to learn about the woman who had been begging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω here means to investigate, inquire about, or learn the story of someone; “to see” is also possible but less fully expresses the curiosity of the crowds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: completely disabled
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρίημι in this passive description indicates a body that has lost its strength or function; “paralyzed” is a possible narrower rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And likewise, when she had been brought in
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμῶς is unusual in this context but can be retained in its sense of “likewise” or “similarly”; no textual correction is required.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as grounds for faith among those standing by
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the healing as serving or producing the faith of those present.

lexical_decisions.chosen: her familiar friend
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθης identifies the friend as her accustomed or close associate, namely Clement’s mother.

passages.text: And then, in this way, Peter spoke about God and the worship that belongs to him, adding at the end: “If anyone wishes to learn these things accurately, let him come to Antioch, where I have decided to remain for several days, and learn the things that lead to his salvation. For surely, while you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and go away to distant places, for eternal salvation you are unwilling to travel even a three-days’ journey.” After Peter’s address, in the presence of the entire crowd, I gave the woman who had been healed one thousand drachmas for provisions and entrusted her to a certain good man who was the foremost citizen of the city and was naturally disposed to do this with joy. After also distributing money to many others and thanking the women who had once comforted my mother, I sailed across to Antaradus together with my mother, Peter, and the remaining companions; and in this way we made our way to our lodging.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the worship that belongs to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφέρειν with the dative can denote what pertains or is proper to someone; θρησκεία here is religious worship or observance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things that lead to his salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός expresses relation or direction toward the hearer’s salvation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἐμπορίας ἕνεκα ἢ στρατείας πατρίδας καταλιμπάνειν οἴδατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: For surely, while you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἴδατε with the infinitive means “you know how”; the negative introduces a rhetorical contrast rather than a straightforward denial.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are unwilling to travel even a three-days’ journey
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive θέλειν creates an abrupt construction after οἴδατε; the translation renders the intended contrast as a finite English clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the foremost citizen of the city
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρῶτος describes the man’s leading civic standing, not merely his chronological position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φύσει μετὰ χαρᾶς τοῦτο ποιεῖν προῃρημένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: was naturally disposed to do this with joy
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαιρεῖσθαι here denotes settled willingness or inclination, qualified by φύσει.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Antaradus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἀντάραδος is the conventional English form of the place-name.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we made our way to our lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία denotes guest lodging or quarters, and ὁρμάω here means to set out or proceed toward them.

source_issues.source_quote: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν
source_issues.issue: The infinitive θέλειν is syntactically abrupt where a finite verb would make the contrast straightforward. The supplied reading is nevertheless intelligible as an anacoluthon or as a continuation of the preceding infinitival construction and has been preserved in translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλετε

passages.text: When we had arrived ... and had partaken of food and given thanks as usual, while there was still time, I said to Peter, “My lord Peter, my mother performed an act of love for humanity when she remembered the woman who had hosted her.” Peter answered, “Do you really think, Clement, that the woman who bore you has performed an act of love for humanity, in that she repaid the woman who received her after the shipwreck? Or did you make this statement as one bestowing a great favor on your mother? If, however, you spoke not as one showing favor but as one telling the truth, you seem to me not to understand what the greatness of love for humanity actually is. It is affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it. Nor do I dare call the hostess who received the woman who bore you after the shipwreck a lover of humanity on that account. For, cajoled by pity, she had been persuaded to become the benefactor of a woman who had suffered shipwreck, was mourning children, was a foreigner, was naked, was alone, and was bitterly lamenting her disasters. Since she was amid so many disasters, who, even among the impious, would not have pitied her on seeing her? Consequently, even the hostess does not appear to have performed in this way an act of love for humanity, but to have acted under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters. How much more, then, did the woman who bore you—after acquiring abundant means and repaying her hostess—perform an act not of love for humanity, but of friendship? There is a great difference between friendship and love for humanity: friendship arises from repayment, whereas love for humanity, without anything that naturally prompts it, loves and benefits every human being insofar as that one is human. If, then, the hostess who showed pity had also pitied and benefited enemies who had wronged her, she would have been a lover of humanity. But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason, such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: When we had arrived ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: γενομένων ἡμῶν can describe the party’s arrival or presence, but the printed lacuna removes its following specification; the three dots are therefore retained without restoration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an act of love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expanded rendering preserves the etymological and argumentative connection among φιλανθρωπία, φιλάνθρωπος, and the later contrast with φιλία.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as one bestowing a great favor on your mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter asks whether Clement’s judgment was an indulgent compliment to his mother rather than a true classification of her act.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἄνευ τοῦ φυσικῶς πείθοντος πρὸς οἱονδήποτε στοργὴ καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter defines love for humanity as affection grounded solely in the recipient’s humanity, without a natural or circumstantial inducement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For, cajoled by pity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the personifying force of κολακεύω: pity flatters, coaxes, or cajoles the hostess into action.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ ἐλέου τοῦ ἐπὶ μυρίαις συμφοραῖς πρὸς εὐεργεσίας κεκινημένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle most naturally modifies ἐλέου, personifying pity itself as moved toward doing good by the accumulation of misfortunes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ μὲν φιλία ἐξ ἀμοιβῆς γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: friendship arises from repayment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμοιβή can mean repayment, return, or reciprocity; “repayment” keeps the immediate connection with the mother’s recompense to her hostess.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ διὰ τί φίλη ἡ ἐχθρὰ καὶ διὰ τί ἐχθρὰ ἡ φίλη
lexical_decisions.chosen: But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: διὰ τί may be interrogative, “why,” or causal, “for some reason.” The causal reading best continues the contrast between unconditional regard for a human being and attachment produced by a particular cause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ τοιαύτη τοῦ τινὸς αἰτίου φίλη ἐστὶν ἢ ἐχθρά, οὐ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
lexical_decisions.chosen: such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s compressed genitive contrast. Alternatively, it may mean that such a person is friend or enemy because of some particular cause, not because the other is human.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints exactly three dots after γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν, marking unavailable content. The gap is retained exactly in the English, and no restoration has been supplied.
The printed period interrupts the phrase φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον. It has been treated as editorial punctuation rather than as a break in the syntax; no Greek word has been altered.
The printed period separates the modal particle ἄν from the verb ἦν. The translation reads the words continuously as a normal contrary-to-fact construction while preserving every printed word.
